\chapter{Numbers Eleven to Twenty}
\label{ch:pt-numbers-eleven-to-twenty}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from eleven to twenty in Portuguese and read dezesseis as the little sentence ten-and-six that it is.}

Run onze to vinte, hear dez e seis inside dezesseis, and note that Portuguese breaks from the fused teens at 16, a number earlier than French or Italian.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[onze — quinze]{onze $\to$ quinze — the short list}

\label{lesson:PT-C12-numeros-11-15}



\begin{quote}
Portuguese inherited the same welded Latin teens as its sisters — but it kept \textbf{fewer of them than anyone}. Just \textbf{five}. After \emph{quinze} (15), it starts over with a completely different, much plainer method.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: The five fusions}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Portuguese} & \textbf{$\leftarrow$ Latin} & \textbf{build} \\
\midrule
11 & \textbf{onze} & \emph{ūndecim} & \textquotedblleft{}one-ten\textquotedblright{} \\
12 & \textbf{doze} & \emph{duodecim} & \textquotedblleft{}two-ten\textquotedblright{} \\
13 & \textbf{treze} & \emph{trēdecim} & \textquotedblleft{}three-ten\textquotedblright{} \\
14 & \textbf{catorze} & \emph{quattuordecim} & \textquotedblleft{}four-ten\textquotedblright{} \\
15 & \textbf{quinze} & \emph{quīndecim} & \textquotedblleft{}five-ten\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The shared \textbf{-ze} is Latin \textbf{decem} (\textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{}) worn thin — the same ten inside \textbf{dez} (10) and \textbf{dezembro} (the old 10th month, from Chapter 9). The digit sits at the front: \emph{dois$\to$do-}, \emph{três$\to$tre-}, \emph{quatro$\to$cator-}, \emph{cinco$\to$quin-}.

Note \textbf{catorze} — Portuguese kept the \emph{c-} where Spanish says \emph{catorce} and French \emph{quatorze}; three worn-down versions of one Latin \emph{quattuordecim}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: And that's where it stops}]
\emph{Quinze} is the \textbf{last} fused number. From \textbf{16} Portuguese does something none of its sisters do so early — the next lesson.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}onze, doze, treze, catorze, quinze\textquotedblright{}
  \item the ten inside — \textquotedblleft{}-ze = \emph{decem} = \textbf{dez}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the digit inside — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{três} $\to$ \textbf{tre}ze, \textbf{cinco} $\to$ \textbf{quin}ze\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count 11 to 15. (\emph{Onze, doze, treze, catorze, quinze}.) What is the \textbf{-ze}? (Latin \textbf{decem}, \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} — as in \emph{dez}, \emph{dezembro}.) How many fused teens does Portuguese keep, and is that more or fewer than its sisters? (\textbf{Five} — \textbf{fewer}; French and Italian keep six.) Next: \textbf{16}, where Portuguese starts building numbers a brand-new way.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dezesseis — vinte]{dezesseis $\to$ vinte — built from scratch, with the \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{} still showing}

\label{lesson:PT-C12-numeros-16-20}



\begin{quote}
At \textbf{16}, Portuguese stops inheriting and starts \textbf{building}. And it does it more openly than any sister: it glues together the living words for \textquotedblleft{}ten,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}and,\textquotedblright{} and the digit — and leaves the \textbf{and} right there in the middle where you can hear it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Ten AND six}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Portuguese} & \textbf{build} & \textbf{literally} \\
\midrule
15 & \textbf{quinze} & (fused, inherited) & \textquotedblleft{}five-ten\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{16} & \textbf{dezesseis} & \textbf{dez + e + seis} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}ten and six\textquotedblright{}} \\
17 & \textbf{dezessete} & dez + e + sete & \textquotedblleft{}ten and seven\textquotedblright{} \\
18 & \textbf{dezoito} & dez + oito & \textquotedblleft{}ten eight\textquotedblright{} \\
19 & \textbf{dezenove} & dez + e + nove & \textquotedblleft{}ten and nine\textquotedblright{} \\
20 & \textbf{vinte} & $\leftarrow$ \emph{vīgintī} & — \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every one begins with \textbf{dez} (\textquotedblleft{}ten,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 6) and most keep \textbf{e} (\textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}) — so \emph{dezesseis} is transparently a little sentence: \emph{ten-and-six}. (\emph{Dezoito} swallows the \emph{e} before the vowel of \emph{oito}.) You already know every ingredient; nothing here needs memorising, only assembling.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: Portuguese breaks earliest}]
All three Romance sisters give up fusing partway through the teens — but Portuguese gives up \textbf{first}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{last fused} & \textbf{goes transparent at} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Portuguese} & \emph{quinze} (15) & \textbf{16} — \emph{dezesseis} \\
French & \emph{seize} (16) & 17 — \emph{dix-sept} \\
Italian & \emph{sedici} (16) & 17 — \emph{diciassette} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One inherited Latin system, three different breaking points — and Portuguese is the boldest rebuilder. (German, by contrast, never breaks at all.)

\textbf{vinte} (20) $\leftarrow$ \emph{vīgintī}, the same root as French \emph{vingt}, Italian \emph{venti}, and English \textbf{vigesimal}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item 15$\to$20 — \textquotedblleft{}quinze, dezesseis, dezessete, dezoito, dezenove, vinte\textquotedblright{}
  \item hear the sentence — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{dez} \textbf{e} \emph{seis} — ten AND six\textquotedblright{}
  \item the whole run, onze to vinte
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{dezesseis} literally spell out? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Ten and six}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{dez} + \emph{e} + \emph{seis}.) At which number does Portuguese break, and how does that compare with French and Italian? (At \textbf{16} — \textbf{earlier}; they break at 17.) Why does \emph{dezoito} have no \emph{e}? (It's \textbf{swallowed} before the vowel of \emph{oito}.) Next chapter: numbers in use.
\end{tcolorbox}
